how-to-compare-financial-aid-offers.html.text:
Financial Aid Award Letter Comparator · guide

How to compare financial aid offers

An award letter mixes four different things under one heading: money you never repay, money you repay with interest, a job, and the bill itself. To compare two letters, sort every line into one of those, then price the loans. This guide does it on three made-up offers, the same ones the comparator loads as its example.

1. Sort the lines

  • Grants and scholarships reduce the price. Check whether each one renews, and on what condition (usually a minimum grade point average).
  • Loans (subsidized, unsubsidized, Parent PLUS, private) do not reduce the price. They move it into the future and add interest.
  • Work-study is the most you can earn, if you find and work the hours.
  • Cost of attendance is the bill plus an estimate of books and living costs. Compare it across colleges on the same lines.

2. The worked example

OfferSticker, 4 yrsNet price, year 1Net price, years 2-4 (avg)BorrowedTotal cost to family
State University$112,958$23,000$24,653$22,000$99,099
Regional University$161,070$27,500$29,857$22,000$127,211
Private College A$269,844$27,500$40,448$54,000$179,870

Assumptions: costs rise 3% a year, loans and work-study repeat each year, 2025-26 federal rates, 10-year repayment. All figures are made up.

Regional University and Private College A show the same $27,500 net price in year 1. That is the number most families compare. But Private College A's letter includes $9,000 of first-year-only aid, so from year 2 the net price climbs to about $40,448 a year, and it fills the gap with $54,000 of loans against $22,000. Over four years the family pays about $52,659 more than at Regional University once loan interest is counted.

3. Use the gap in an appeal

If the cheapest offer is not the college you want, the useful question is how far apart the offers really are. In the example Private College A would need about $18,950 more in grants each year to match State University. A financial aid appeal that shows a competing offer and an exact gap is easier to act on than a request for more aid. Whether an office agrees is up to it.

Open the comparator, replace the example with your letters, and change the rates to the ones that apply to you.

Questions

What is the difference between net price and total cost?

Net price is the cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships: what the college bills you after gift aid. Total cost also counts what the loans will cost you to repay, so a college that fills the gap with loans looks the same as one that fills it with grants on net price alone, and is much dearer in total.

Which of the three example colleges is cheapest?

With the made-up numbers on this page, State University costs $99,099 in total, Regional University $127,211 and Private College A $179,870. Private College A and Regional University both show a $27,500 net price in year 1, but Private College A's net price rises to about $40,448 a year from year 2 because $9,000 of its aid is first-year only, and it comes with $54,000 of loans.

How much more grant would Private College A need to match State University?

About $18,950 more in grants each year in the example. That figure is what to bring to a financial aid appeal: a competing offer and the exact gap, rather than a request for 'more aid'.

Do I have to accept every loan on the letter?

No. Loans on an award letter are offers. You can accept part of a loan or decline it. Borrowing more than the bill, or more than the net price after work-study, is borrowing money you do not need, and the tool flags it.

FINANCIAL AID AWARD LETTER COMPARATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which college offer will really cost less?

Type in what each award letter says and see the true four-year cost of every offer. Only grants and scholarships cut the price. Loans are a bill that arrives later with interest, and work-study is a job. The tool adds up what your family pays in cash and in loan payments, catches first-year-only scholarships that make year 2 jump, and works out the extra grant that would make a dearer offer match the cheapest one.

The example below is made-up numbers, not a real letter. New to this? Read how to compare financial aid offers, with a worked example.

1. Your offers

One block per college, a blank line between blocks. Use label: amount lines. Known labels: College, Tuition and fees, Housing and food, Books and other (or one Cost of attendance total), Grants and scholarships, One-time first-year grant, Work-study, Subsidized loan, Unsubsidized loan, Parent PLUS, Private loan. Lines starting with # are ignored.

2. Assumptions (edit these)

Rates and fees start at 2025-26 federal figures. Replace them with the rates for the year you borrow (studentaid.gov); private loan terms are on your lender's offer.

3. What each offer really costs

Questions

How do I compare financial aid award letters?

Put the same four things from each letter side by side: the full cost of attendance, the grants and scholarships (money you never repay), the loans (money you repay with interest) and work-study (money you earn by working). Subtract only the grants from the cost to get the net price, then add what the loans will cost you over their repayment. This tool does that for every offer and ranks them by total cost to your family.

Are loans and work-study financial aid I should subtract from the price?

Not as a price cut. Loans are borrowed money that you repay, usually with interest, so they move the bill into the future. Work-study is a job: the amount is the most you can earn, only if you find and work the hours. Only grants and scholarships reduce what the college costs you. The tool shows loans and work-study separately for that reason.

What is a first-year-only scholarship and why does it matter?

Some award letters include a grant that applies to the first year only, or one that renews only if you keep a minimum grade point average. Year 1 then looks cheap and years 2 to 4 cost much more. Enter a non-renewing grant on its own line (One-time first-year grant) and the tool shows how the net price steps up from year 2.

How is the cost of the loans worked out?

Each year's loans are assumed to be borrowed at the start of the year. Subsidized loans add no interest while you are in school; the other loans add simple interest until repayment starts, after a grace period you can set. The balance is then repaid in equal monthly payments over the term you choose, at the rate you enter. Origination fees are counted as cash you pay. Rates and fees start at 2025-26 federal values and you should replace them with the ones that apply to you.

What does 'grant needed to match' mean, and can I use it to appeal an offer?

It is the extra gift aid per year that would bring that offer's total cost down to the cheapest offer, with any loan you no longer need dropped. It is a number to start a conversation: many financial aid offices will look at a written appeal that shows a competing offer or a change in your family's circumstances. The tool does not know whether any office will agree.

Is this financial advice, and is my information uploaded?

No to both. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, not financial, tax or legal advice, and it is not affiliated with any college or with the U.S. Department of Education. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and nothing is saved when you close the page.

Why does the cheapest sticker price not always win?

Because the sticker price is before aid. A college with a high published price and a large renewing grant can cost less than a cheaper-looking college that offers loans instead of grants. The comparison that matters is the total you will pay, in cash during school and in loan payments afterwards.
